summary.text: 告 commonly means “tell,” “report,” “announce,” “inform,” or “accuse.” Its early graphic construction is disputed: one proposal derives it from 舌 by extending the central stroke upward to depict a tongue projecting from a mouth and connect it with speaking or telling; other accounts analyze 牛 plus 口, or 口 plus an abbreviated 壴.

formation.text: The formation is disputed. One proposal treats the whole graph as a pictorial form derived from 舌: its central stroke is extended upward to depict a tongue projecting from a mouth, associated with speaking or telling. The received Shuowen account analyzes 牛 plus 口 and explains an ox striking a person while a crossbar restrains its horns as a way of signaling people. A separate proposal analyzes 口 plus an abbreviated 壴; 壴 may be phonetic and possibly semantic, but its function is uncertain.

history.text: The received Shuowen explanation analyzes 告 as 牛 plus 口 and interprets it as an ox striking a person while a crossbar restrains its horns, thereby informing people. This historical lexicographic account does not confirm the construction of earlier forms.

A later graphic account describes the seal form as abbreviated during clerical transformation and regularized into the modern form. The curated image is a modern redraw of the seal form transmitted in the Shuowen tradition; it illustrates that later form but does not settle competing explanations of earlier forms.

uncertainties.text: The early construction remains unresolved among a whole-graph tongue picture derived from 舌, the Shuowen 牛-plus-口 explanation, and the reported 口-plus-abbreviated-壴 proposal. The 壴 proposal is available here from an article abstract, and its function is uncertain.

A Southwestern Mandarin word meaning “try” or “check out” is reported as written 告 through borrowing from 校. Similar Middle Chinese readings are reported, but the proposed direction and sound pathway are unverified; the 1909 example attests the regional use, not its derivation.

senses.period: Shang oracle-bone and later examples reported; exact dating unresolved
senses.text: A reported oracle-bone example concerns a deer report, and later examples use 告 for reporting or telling. These attestations do not establish one original meaning or a sequence of semantic change.

senses.period: Western Zhou examples reported; exact dating unresolved
senses.text: Western Zhou bronze examples are reported with uses for reporting and admonishing. Their development from earlier senses is not established.

senses.period: Western Zhou examples reported; exact dating unresolved
senses.text: Accusatory use is reported among Western Zhou bronze examples; its relationship to “report” is not established.
Current uses include telling, announcing, informing, and accusing. The supplied glosses do not establish their chronology or semantic connections.

A Southwestern Mandarin use meaning “try” or “check out” is attested in a 1909 example. One proposed account is that 告 borrowed the graph for 校 to write a similar-sounding word, rather than developing this meaning from “tell.” The borrowing direction and sound pathway remain uncertain.

limitations.text: The cited examples do not establish a sequence connecting sacrificial, reporting, admonishing, accusatory, and telling uses.
The proposed borrowing from 校 lacks independent confirmation of its source account and historical sound pathway; similarity alone does not establish the borrowing direction.

items.period: Shuowen Jiezi Lesser Seal tradition; modern vector file dated 2013-12-09
items.tradition: Small/Lesser Seal (小篆), Shuowen Jiezi radical form
items.caption: A modern redraw of the 告 seal form transmitted in the Shuowen Jiezi tradition. The image shows a vertical stroke crossing a curved upper shape and a box-like lower enclosure; this later form does not settle competing explanations of the graph’s earlier construction.
items.alt: Black seal-script strokes: a central vertical line crosses a curved upper form and a box-like lower enclosure.
items.selection_reason: It provides a visually inspectable example of the later Shuowen seal tradition relevant to the historical ox-and-mouth account, while the competing analyses of earlier forms remain unresolved.

limitations.text: This seal-form redraw does not establish the identity or meaning of the upper element in earlier forms. Analyses remain disputed among a protruding tongue, 牛 plus 口, and an abbreviated 壴 plus 口; the cited accounts do not settle the graph’s origin.
